questions.stem: A deletion mutation removes one base from the middle of a gene. Why is a deletion likely to be more harmful than a substitution of a single base?

options.text: A deletion changes only one amino acid, while a substitution changes many
A deletion causes a frameshift, changing every codon and amino acid downstream, while a substitution typically affects only one amino acid
Deletions only affect non-coding DNA, while substitutions affect genes
Deletions always cause cancer, while substitutions do not

questions.explanation: DNA is read in triplets (codons). Deleting one base shifts the reading frame for every subsequent triplet, changing potentially every amino acid from that point onwards (frameshift mutation). A substitution typically changes only the one codon where it occurs, affecting just one amino acid. This is why deletions usually cause more severe changes to protein structure and function.

questions.stem: UV radiation from the sun can cause mutations in skin cells. A person who works outdoors for many years develops skin cancer. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: UV radiation caused mutations in genes that control cell division, leading to uncontrolled cell growth
UV radiation destroyed all the DNA in the skin cells
The person inherited the skin cancer from their parents
UV radiation caused the skin cells to stop dividing

questions.explanation: UV radiation is a mutagen that can cause mutations in the DNA of skin cells. If mutations occur in genes that regulate cell division (proto-oncogenes or tumour suppressor genes), cells may begin to divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour. Multiple mutations typically accumulate over years of exposure before cancer develops. This is why sun protection is important.

questions.stem: Most mutations are neutral and have no effect on the organism. Which explanation best accounts for why many mutations are harmless?

options.text: Most mutations are repaired by the cell before they can cause any harm
The genetic code is degenerate (redundant), so some base changes still code for the same amino acid (silent mutations)
Mutations only occur in non-essential parts of the body
The immune system destroys all cells with mutations

questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning multiple codons can code for the same amino acid (e.g., GCU, GCC, GCA, and GCG all code for alanine). If a substitution changes a base but the new codon still codes for the same amino acid, the protein is unchanged. These are called silent mutations. Additionally, many mutations occur in non-coding DNA regions.

questions.stem: Sickle cell disease is caused by a single base substitution in the gene for haemoglobin, changing one amino acid. How can such a small change cause such a serious disease?

options.text: The substitution deletes the entire haemoglobin gene
The changed amino acid alters the shape of the haemoglobin protein, causing it to form rigid structures that distort red blood cells into a sickle shape
The mutation prevents red blood cells from being produced at all
The mutation affects every amino acid in the haemoglobin chain

questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, a single amino acid change (glutamic acid to valine) alters the tertiary structure of haemoglobin. The abnormal haemoglobin molecules stick together in low-oxygen conditions, forming rigid fibres that distort red blood cells into a sickle shape. These cells block capillaries, reducing oxygen delivery. This shows how one amino acid can critically affect protein function.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell of an adult human. Can this mutation be passed on to their children?

options.text: Yes, because all mutations are inherited
Yes, but only if the mutation causes cancer
No, because only mutations in gametes (sex cells) or cells that produce gametes can be inherited
No, because mutations in adults cannot affect their DNA

questions.explanation: Only mutations in gametes (eggs or sperm) or in the cells that produce them can be passed to offspring. Mutations in body (somatic) cells like skin cells affect only the individual and are not inherited. A skin cell mutation might cause problems for that person (e.g., skin cancer), but it will not appear in their children's DNA.
